## Boxplots of the quantitative variables
```{r box plot}
quant_vars <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  select(`2022 Population`, starts_with("Area"), starts_with("Density"),
         `Growth Rate`, `World Population Percentage`)
### long format so one boxplot is drawn per variable
quant_vars %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "", y = "", title = "Boxplots of quantitative variables")


```
### Counting outliers in each variable
```{r count-outliers}
quant_vars %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ length(boxplot.stats(.x)$out)))


```
## Handling missing values and outliers
```{r handle-na-outliers}
## missing values: replace with the column median (only matters if the check above shows any)
world_pop_cleaned <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ replace_na(.x, median(.x, na.rm = TRUE))))

## function that caps values at the boxplot limits (winsorization)
winsorize <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  fence <- 1.5 * (q[2] - q[1])
  pmin(pmax(x, q[1] - fence), q[2] + fence)
}

## capped values go into NEW columns ending in _capped, originals stay unchanged
world_pop_cleaned <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  mutate(across(c(`2022 Population`, starts_with("Area"), starts_with("Density"),
                  `Growth Rate`, `World Population Percentage`),
                winsorize, .names = "{.col}_capped"))
```
##  Population projection for 2030 using Nt = P * e^(r*t)
```{r projection-2030}
## Growth Rate is a multiplier (e.g. 1.01), so r = Growth Rate - 1
## t = number of years from 2022 to 2030
t_years <- 2030 - 2022

world_pop_cleaned <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  mutate(r = `Growth Rate` - 1,
         Pop2030 = round(`2022 Population` * exp(r * t_years)))

## preview the result
world_pop_cleaned %>%
  select(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`, r, Pop2030) %>%
  head(10)
```
##  Top ten countries by 2022 population
```{r top10}
top10 <- world_pop_cleaned %>% slice_max(`2022 Population`, n = 10)

ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`),
                  y = `2022 Population` / 1e6)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 10 most populous countries, 2022",
       x = "Country", y = "Population (millions)") +
  theme_minimal()

```
## Population trend 1990 to 2022 for the top ten
```{r top10-trend}
## the $ in the pattern keeps only the original year columns, not the _capped ones
top10_trend <- top10 %>%
  select(`Country/Territory`, matches("^\\d{4} Population$")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-`Country/Territory`, names_to = "year", values_to = "population") %>%
  mutate(year = parse_number(year))

ggplot(top10_trend, aes(x = year, y = population / 1e6, colour = `Country/Territory`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Population trend of the top 10 countries, 1990-2022",
       x = "Year", y = "Population (millions)", colour = "Country") +
  theme_minimal()
```
## The CO2 file has two columns for 2019, check if they are identical
```{r check-co2-names}
names(CO2_emission)
all(CO2_emission$`2019...34` == CO2_emission$`2019...35`, na.rm = TRUE)
```
## If the result above is TRUE, keep one 2019 column and name it 2019
```{r clean-co2}
CO2_emission <- CO2_emission %>%
  select(-`2019...35`) %>%
  rename(`2019` = `2019...34`)

```
## CO2 emission trend 1990 to 2019 for the top ten countries
```{r co2-trend}
co2_top10 <- CO2_emission %>%
  filter(country_code %in% top10$CCA3) %>%
  pivot_longer(matches("^\\d{4}$"), names_to = "year", values_to = "co2") %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

ggplot(co2_top10, aes(x = year, y = co2, colour = `Country Name`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "CO2 emissions of the top 10 populous countries, 1990-2019",
       x = "Year", y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita)", colour = "Country") +
  theme_minimal()
```
##  Correlation: Area, Density, Growth Rate, World Population Percentage
```{r correlation}
cor_data <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  select(starts_with("Area"), starts_with("Density"),
         `Growth Rate`, `World Population Percentage`) %>%
  select(-ends_with("_capped"))

## numerical correlation matrix
cor_mat <- round(cor(cor_data, use = "complete.obs"), 2)
cor_mat

## heatmap of the same matrix
cor_mat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") %>%
  ggplot(aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = r)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation heatmap", x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```
##  Merging population (2022) and CO2 (2019)
```{r merge}
## join on the 3-letter country code because country names differ between the files
pop_small <- world_pop_cleaned %>%
  select(CCA3, `Country/Territory`, Continent, `2022 Population`)

co2_small <- CO2_emission %>%
  select(CCA3 = country_code, CO2_2019 = `2019`)

merged <- inner_join(pop_small, co2_small, by = "CCA3") %>%
  filter(!is.na(CO2_2019)) %>%
  mutate(Pop_millions = `2022 Population` / 1e6)

nrow(merged)

## Relationship between population and CO2 emissions

```{r }

## scatter plot with population on a log scale and a regression line

ggplot(merged, aes(Pop_millions, CO2_2019)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkblue") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Population (log scale) vs CO2 per capita, 2019",
       x = "Population in millions (log10)", y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

## Pearson, Spearman and Pearson with logged population

cor(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_2019)
cor(merged$Pop_millions, merged$CO2_2019, method = "spearman")
cor(log10(merged$Pop_millions), merged$CO2_2019)

## simple linear regression

summary(lm(CO2_2019 ~ log10(Pop_millions), data = merged))

```
## Comparing CO2 emissions by continent

```{r continent}

## sum of 2019 CO2 by continent, highest first

continent_co2 <- merged %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarise(total_co2 = sum(CO2_2019)) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_co2))
continent_co2

ggplot(continent_co2, aes(reorder(Continent, total_co2), total_co2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Total 2019 CO2 emissions by continent",
       x = "Continent", y = "Sum of CO2 (metric tons per capita)") +
  theme_minimal()

## answers to the three questions

slice(continent_co2, 1)            ## highest continent
slice(continent_co2, 3)            ## third continent and its total
slice_tail(continent_co2, n = 1)   ## last continent and its total
```
